text: There is a tempting excuse: Carrick inherited a squad assembled for incompatible managers. That is partly true. But it is no longer the whole truth. United gave him a contract through 2028. The hierarchy led by Omar Berrada and Jason Wilcox rebuilt the midfield with Andrey Santos, Youri Tielemans and Carlos Baleba. Carrick now owns part of the solution and part of the problem. A modern football structure should recruit for principles that outlast the coach: how the team builds, presses, protects the centre, and responds after losing the ball. If those principles are clear, a new manager adjusts the model. If they are not, every appointment becomes demolition followed by another expensive rebuild. Recruitment is where the tactical argument becomes an institutional one. A club does not need every player to fit one manager's favourite formation, but it does need a repeatable idea about distances, pressing, progression and defensive cover. Otherwise each transfer window solves the last coach's problem and creates the next coach's problem. Carrick can improve the team, but he cannot personally reconcile years of contradictory squad-building. That responsibility belongs to the football structure around him.
